title: What does a consultant actually do all day?
description: A realistic look at a junior consultant's day and week: analysis, slides, client meetings, team problem solving, travel and the hours involved.
hook: A junior consultant spends most of the day analysing data, talking to people who know the business, turning findings into slides and working out with the team what it all means for the client. The exact mix changes by project and by week, but that rhythm of analysis, discussion and communication is common to almost every firm. Here is what it looks like in practice, including the parts that do not make the recruiting brochures.
body:
The five things you actually spend time on

  • Analysis. Much of the week goes into spreadsheets and data: cleaning a sales file, building a simple model, checking whether a hypothesis survives contact with the numbers.
  • Interviews. Speaking to the client's managers and front-line staff, customers, suppliers or outside experts to learn what the data does not show.
  • Slides. Turning findings into charts with a one-sentence headline that states the insight ("Failed deliveries cost $21M a year, mostly in three regions"), not a label ("Failed deliveries by region").
  • Team problem solving. Short sessions with your manager, and sometimes a partner, to decide what the findings mean and what to do next.
  • Client meetings. Working sessions with the client team, plus regular updates to senior executives, often a steering committee every few weeks.

Junior consultants usually own one piece of the problem, a workstream, and are responsible for its analysis and slides from start to finish. That ownership comes early, which is one of the main attractions of the job.

One workstream from Monday to Friday

Suppose your team is helping a parcel carrier reduce failed deliveries, where the driver cannot hand over the parcel and has to try again. Your week might run like this.

DayWhat you do
MondayTravel to the client, plan the week with the team, clean the shipment data and check whether failures cluster by area or time of day.
TuesdayInterview three depot managers and ride along with a driver to see why deliveries fail.
WednesdaySize the cost of redelivery and test two hypotheses in a problem-solving session with your manager.
ThursdayCompare fixes such as better address checks or delivery-time windows; review draft findings with the client team and rework the analysis after their questions.
FridayWork from your home office, finish the slides for next week's steering committee and agree a pilot with the client.

The work is iterative. A slide might start as a hypothesis and change three times as the data contradicts it.

The numbers behind Wednesday

Here is the kind of sizing you would do, with illustrative numbers. The carrier makes 1.5M deliveries a week, and 6% fail at the first attempt.

  • Failed deliveries: 1.5M × 6% = 90,000 a week.
  • At $4.50 per redelivery: 90,000 × $4.50 = $405k a week.
  • Over a year: $405k × 52 ≈ $21.1M.
  • Against total delivery costs of $600M, that is about 3.5%.

Now the "so what". If better address checks would cut failures by a third, the saving is about $21.1M ÷ 3 ≈ $7.0M a year. A $2.5M software project would pay back in roughly four months. That is worth a pilot.

Part of the job is also knowing when to stop. If failures had been 0.5% of costs, the right move would be to tell your manager the workstream is unlikely to matter and suggest the team's time goes elsewhere. Good consultants manage detail, but they also focus on what moves the answer.

Where the work happens, and the hours

Often at the client's offices for part of the week, especially on larger projects, and in your own office or at home for the rest. Travel varies a great deal by firm, office, industry and project: some consultants travel most weeks, others rarely leave their city.

Long hours are common, especially before a big presentation, and they vary by project and manager. Rather than relying on reputation, ask people at each firm what a typical week looks like in the office you would join, and how often that changes. Networking conversations are the right place for that question.

What people enjoy, and what they find hard

People who enjoy the job usually mention:

  • learning fast, with a new industry or problem every few months;
  • smart, motivated colleagues;
  • seeing how senior leaders make decisions, early in a career;
  • regular feedback and a structured path to grow.

The common frustrations are long or unpredictable hours and travel, moving on before you see the results of your work, and pressure to perform and be promoted on a set timeline (see the consulting career path).

How the job maps to the case interview

Every stage of a case is a small rehearsal of the week above. Structuring is planning the work. The maths is Wednesday's sizing. Reading a chart is reviewing the data. The recommendation is the steering committee. Interviewers are asking whether they would trust you with a workstream.

Compare two ways of reporting the parcel sizing.

"Failed deliveries are 90,000 a week and cost $4.50 each, so $405,000 a week."
"Failed deliveries cost about $21M a year, roughly 3.5% of delivery costs. If address checks cut failures by a third, that is $7M a year, so a $2.5M fix pays back in about four months. I'd test it in one region first."

Both are correct. Only the second explains the consequence and proposes a next step, which is what a manager wants from a junior consultant. Practise that habit with so-what thinking.

Practice

1. If failures fell from 6% to 4% of 1.5M weekly deliveries, what is the annual saving at $4.50 per redelivery?

Show the answer

Failures fall by 2 points: 1.5M × 2% = 30,000 a week. Saving = 30,000 × $4.50 = $135k a week, or $135k × 52 ≈ $7.0M a year. That matches the "cut by a third" estimate, since 2 points is a third of 6%.

2. Your manager asks for a slide headline on the sizing. Write one.

Show the answer

"Failed deliveries cost about $21M a year; address checks could save a third of that." It states the finding and its implication in one sentence, so an executive who reads only the headline still gets the point.

Where to go next

Read the types of consulting to see how this week changes in strategy, operations and technology work, then practise the sizing habit in the maths drills.
